processing: Pu-erh, in shops mostly ripe, flavoured with the leaves of Strobilanthes tonkinensis, either pressed in with the tea or used to scent it, much as jasmine scents green tea.
harvest_season: Not a matter of season on the label. The tea base follows ordinary pu-erh pickings, and one sold brick states autumn-picked ripe tea.
appearance_dry: Small dark brown tuos or bricks, sometimes with flecks of dried green-brown herb, and a strong smell of cooked sticky rice.
appearance_liquor: Dark reddish brown and clear, as with other ripe pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Soft dark brown leaf, with bits of darker herb leaf where it was pressed in.
taste_profile: Ripe pu-erh smoothness under a sweet, toasty aroma of freshly steamed sticky rice, which is strongest in the early steeps.

brewing.notes: Rinse quickly. A whole mini tuo often suits a mug or small pot; break it up in a gaiwan if you want more steeps. The rice aroma goes first, so do not leave the early steeps long.

vintage_note: Sold with a production year, often as mini tuos or bricks, with lots from 2012, 2018 and 2020 all on the market. The year matters less than with plain pu-erh, because this is a flavoured everyday tea. Aromatic herbs generally fade, so a recent tea stored sealed is the sensible choice over an old one.
description:
There is no rice in this tea. The smell of steamed sticky rice comes from a plant, Strobilanthes tonkinensis, whose leaves carry that aroma remarkably well. It grows in southern Yunnan and is associated with Mengla in Xishuangbanna.

Makers use it in two ways. The simpler one presses the dried herb together with the tea, much as tangerine peel is combined with pu-erh. The other uses the leaf's readiness to absorb smell and scents it with the herb, closer to how jasmine tea is made.

The first steeps are all aroma: sweet, toasty and very like a rice cooker just opened. Then the ordinary ripe tea takes over, soft and earthy. People tend to either love it or find it artificial, so try a single mini tuo before buying a stack.

Most of what you will find is small tuos or bricks, and the base tea is rarely the point. Look for a clean smell without mustiness, and for a stated year.
history:
Little is documented about when this herb was first combined with pu-erh, or by whom.

As a commercial product it is well established today, sold by Western and Chinese tea shops mainly as mini tuos and bricks. Descriptions of where the herb and the tea come from vary between sellers: Mengla and Xishuangbanna for the plant, with the finished tea sometimes labelled Menghai or Kunming.
